title: India Has 745 Million Football Fans. Until Last Week, None of Them Had a Way to Watch the World Cup.
excerpt: A last-minute broadcast deal, Kerala's streets lined with giant banners, and the challenge of watching from America — inside the Indian fan experience as the biggest World Cup in history kicks off
body:
The biggest FIFA World Cup in history begins this week across the United States, Canada, and Mexico — 48 teams, 104 matches, six weeks of football. And until just days ago, the 745 million Indians who watched the 2022 edition had no way to watch it.

## The Broadcast Crisis Nobody Saw Coming

For weeks leading up to the tournament, FIFA and Indian broadcasters were locked in a deadlock that left the country's massive football fanbase in limbo. No television network. No streaming partner. No deal.

The standoff was not about lack of interest — India produced the second-largest World Cup viewership in the world after China during Qatar 2022, a number that stunned even FIFA's own analysts. It was about money. Indian broadcasters balked at the rights fee for a tournament their national team was not competing in, while FIFA held firm on valuations that reflected India's audience size rather than its team's absence.

The resolution came at the eleventh hour. ZEE's digital and television networks struck a deal with FIFA, giving Indian fans access through the Zee5 app and a brand-new television network: Unite8 Sports. Four channels — Unite8 Sports 1 and 2 in both standard and HD, offering Hindi and English commentary — will carry every match. On mobile, the Zee5 "All Access + Sports" three-month plan costs ₹799 (roughly $9.50), covering the entire tournament.

For NRIs in the diaspora, the relief is real but the logistics are surprisingly favourable. Most group-stage matches kick off between 10 PM and 3 AM IST, which translates to afternoon and evening slots in American time zones — a rare alignment that actually benefits the diaspora over fans back home. For once, Indian Americans will not need to set 3 AM alarms. The tournament starts with Mexico versus South Africa on June 11 (June 12 IST), with the final on July 19.

## Kerala Is Already a Different Country

In Malappuram and Palakkad, the transformation has begun. Giant banners of Neymar's Brazil squad stretch across roads, carried by fans setting off yellow flares and beating drums. Neighbouring communities have split into rival fan groups — Brazil against Argentina, France against Germany, Spain against the Netherlands — each claiming a stretch of road as their team's territory.

This is not new. Kerala's obsession with football, particularly with Brazil and Argentina, predates modern streaming and satellite television. What is new is the scale. The 2026 World Cup's expansion from 32 to 48 teams has drawn nations that Kerala's fans have adopted informally for years — Morocco, Ivory Coast, Japan — into the main draw. The tournament format now features 12 groups of four, with the top two and the eight best third-placed teams advancing to a new Round of 32.

## The Expanded Tournament, Explained

The numbers are staggering. Twelve groups instead of eight. A Round of 32 before the Round of 16. One hundred and four matches across 16 host cities spanning three countries and four time zones. For fans following from India or the diaspora, this means more football in a single tournament than any World Cup has ever offered.

The group stage alone stretches across three weeks. For NRIs in the US, the host cities are significant — matches in New Jersey, Dallas, Houston, Miami, Seattle, Los Angeles, Atlanta, and the Bay Area are within driving distance of major Indian American population centres. Community watch parties are already being organised in cities with large diaspora populations, and state governments are funding public screenings.

## What to Watch For

India is not on the pitch, but its connections to the tournament run deeper than absence. Four players with Indian heritage will take the field for four different nations — a story The Videshi covered earlier this week. Tahsin Mohammed Jamshid, a 19-year-old winger born in Doha to Keralite parents, represents Qatar. Sarpreet Singh, of Punjabi descent, plays for New Zealand.

Lionel Messi and Cristiano Ronaldo are both set for record-breaking sixth World Cup campaigns, an achievement that carries extra weight in a country where allegiance to Argentina or Portugal defines football identity in states from Kerala to Goa. Neymar has hinted this may be his farewell World Cup. These storylines will dominate drawing rooms and group chats across the Indian diaspora for six weeks.

Beyond personal connections, the tournament matters because football is the one global sport where India's absence does not diminish its fans' passion. From the bars of Jersey City to the living rooms of Kozhikode, the next six weeks belong to football.
